name: Kubeless

archived.reason: On 25 August 2021 VMware marked Kubeless as no longer maintained and stopped answering issues and pull requests; the last release, v1.0.8, dates from January 2021 and the repository is now archived read-only under vmware-archive. It was tested only up to Kubernetes 1.15 and no maintained fork took over.

summary: An archived Kubernetes-native functions framework: each function was a custom resource that a controller turned into its own Deployment and Service, triggered over HTTP, by cron or from Kafka, NATS or Kinesis.
intro: Kubeless added a `Function` custom resource to Kubernetes. You deployed code with `kubeless function deploy`, naming a runtime such as Python, Node.js, Go, Ruby, PHP, Java, .NET Core or Ballerina, and a controller in the cluster created a Deployment and a ClusterIP Service for that function. The code itself travelled inside the custom resource and was mounted into the runtime pod from a ConfigMap, with an init container installing its dependencies, so a function’s source had to fit in a single etcd entry of 1 MB.

Every runtime was a small web server (Express for Node.js, Bottle for Python, Sinatra for Ruby) that called a handler taking an `event` and a `context`. Triggers were separate custom resources with their own controllers: an HTTP trigger created an Ingress, a cron trigger a Kubernetes CronJob, and Kafka, NATS and AWS Kinesis triggers ran consumers that called the function for each message. Scaling used a standard HorizontalPodAutoscaler on CPU or requests per second, with at least one pod per function, so there was no scale to zero.

Kubeless was one of the first function frameworks built on Kubernetes custom resources. It started in late 2016 at Skippbox, which Bitnami bought in 2017, and moved to VMware when VMware acquired Bitnami in 2019. VMware stopped maintaining it in August 2021, and the repository has been archived since.
strengths: Functions were plain Kubernetes objects: a custom resource, a Deployment and a Service, visible to kubectl and existing tooling
A uniform `handler(event, context)` interface across languages and across HTTP, cron and message triggers
Simple to read and extend: adding a runtime meant building an image, and each trigger type was its own small controller
limits: Unmaintained since August 2021 and tested only up to Kubernetes 1.15; its runtime images target language versions that have long reached end of life, such as Node.js 8 and Python 3.6
No scale to zero: every function kept at least one pod running
Function code lived inside the custom resource, which capped it at etcd’s 1 MB entry size
Kafka triggers invoked functions at most once, so a failed call could lose a message

story: Kubeless grew out of work by Sebastien Goasguen, founder of the Kubernetes start-up Skippbox; its repository was created in November 2016. The idea was to make functions first-class objects in the cluster, using Kubernetes’ extension mechanism for custom resource types, with a controller that turned each one into ordinary Deployments and Services.

Bitnami bought Skippbox in March 2017 and kept developing Kubeless; in May 2017 RedMonk described it as a serverless framework native to Kubernetes, competing with Fission, funktion, funcatron and OpenWhisk, with functions as custom resources, Node.js and Python runtimes, and Kafka for pub/sub. More languages and triggers followed, and version 1.0 arrived in November 2018.

VMware announced it would acquire Bitnami in May 2019, and Kubeless moved with it. Releases slowed to v1.0.8 in January 2021. On August 25, 2021, VMware added a notice that it no longer maintained the project and invited anyone to take it over as a fork; no fork was linked, the last commit landed in December 2021, and the repository now lives read-only under the vmware-archive organization.

choices.why: Making a function a Kubernetes object let the project reuse Deployments, Services, Ingress and autoscalers instead of building its own scheduler or router.
Each function scaled and failed on its own using standard Kubernetes parts, at the cost of at least one idle pod per function and pod-start cold starts.

choices.choice: Code stored in the custom resource
choices.why: Keeping the source in the Function object meant no separate artifact store or image build was needed for small functions, which also limited code to what fits in etcd.
